items.stem: A common talcum powder contains 4 % m/m zinc oxide, which acts as an antiseptic. How much zinc oxide is present in 300 g of the talcum powder?
items.answer: There are 12 grams of zinc oxide present in the powder. This is calculated using the mass by mass percentage formula, where 4% of the total 300 g mass of the mixture is the zinc oxide solute.

items.stem: Your mother gives you a bottle of orange juice concentrate to mix with water and serve it to your visiting friends. She asks you to mix two tablespoons of the concentrate with water in a glass tumbler. If each tablespoon measures 15 mL and you make 150 mL of juice per person, what is the % v/v of orange juice concentrate in the mixture you prepared?
items.answer: The concentration of the orange juice mixture is 20% v/v. The volume of the solute is 30 mL (two tablespoons of 15 mL each), which is divided by the total volume of the solution (150 mL) and then multiplied by 100 to find the volume by volume percentage.

items.stem: Vinegar, used as a food preservative and additive, contains 5 % v/v acetic acid. Glacial acetic acid is a liquid, i.e., 100% acetic acid. If you want to make vinegar from glacial acetic acid, how would you proceed?
items.answer: To make vinegar, you need to prepare a 5% v/v solution of acetic acid. You would proceed by measuring 5 mL of the glacial acetic acid (solute) and mixing it with enough water (solvent) to reach a total combined volume of 100 mL.

items.stem: Refer to the solubility curves given in Activity 5.2. If equal masses of hot, saturated solutions of compounds ‘A’ and ‘B’ are cooled from 80 degrees C to 60 degrees C, which solution is likely to deposit more solid?
items.answer: The solution of compound ‘B’ is likely to deposit more solid. According to the solubility curves, compound ‘B’ shows a much steeper decrease in solubility as the temperature drops from 80 degrees C to 60 degrees C compared to compound ‘A’, meaning a larger amount of excess solute will crystallize and separate out.

items.stem: Will there be any change in the size of common salt crystals if the rate of evaporation is increased or decreased? Explain.
items.answer: Yes, the rate of evaporation directly affects the size of the crystals formed. If the rate of evaporation is decreased by allowing the solution to cool slowly, the particles have more time to come together and arrange themselves, resulting in larger, well-shaped crystals. Conversely, if evaporation is increased and happens too rapidly, smaller and less well-formed crystals will develop.

items.stem: State whether the following statements are True or False. Also, correct the False statements. (i) Salt can be separated from a salt solution by evaporation or distillation. (ii) Distillation can be used for separation of two liquids even when these have the same boiling point. (iii) In paper chromatography, the solvent level should be above the sample spot at the beginning of the experiment. (iv) Evaporation and crystallization are the same processes.
items.answer: (i) True. (ii) False. Correction: Distillation can only be used to separate two miscible liquids if they have different boiling points, typically requiring a minimum difference of 25 degrees C. (iii) False. Correction: In paper chromatography, the solvent level should be strictly below the sample spot at the beginning of the experiment so that the liquid can slowly carry the substances up the paper rather than dissolving them directly into the bulk solvent. (iv) False. Correction: Evaporation simply involves turning a solvent into vapour to leave behind a solid, which may contain impurities, whereas crystallization is a specific process that yields a pure solid in a regular geometric pattern from a saturated solution.

items.stem: Why do immiscible liquids form two separate layers in a separating funnel?
items.answer: Immiscible liquids form two separate layers because they do not mix together and they possess different densities. When the mixture is left undisturbed, the denser liquid sinks to the bottom to form the lower layer, while the lighter, less dense liquid floats to form the upper layer.

items.stem: Is sublimation different from evaporation? Justify.
items.answer: Yes, sublimation is distinctly different from evaporation. Sublimation is the direct transition of a solid into a vapour without ever passing through a liquid state, whereas evaporation is the transition of a substance from a liquid state into a vapour.

items.stem: Clouds are made up of tiny water droplets or ice crystals floating in the air. Based on what you know about solutions, suspensions and colloids, what type of mixture do you think clouds are and why?
items.answer: Clouds are a type of colloidal mixture, specifically referred to as an aerosol. In this mixture, the tiny water droplets or ice crystals act as the dispersed phase which is suspended evenly throughout the air, serving as the dispersion medium. Unlike suspensions, these tiny particles do not settle down under the influence of gravity over time.

items.stem: Why do cities with a lot of smoke and dust in the air often look hazy?
items.answer: Cities with significant smoke and dust look hazy because of the Tyndall effect. The fine dust and smoke particles suspended in the atmosphere act as colloidal particles. When sunlight passes through the air, these particles scatter the light in all directions, making the path of light visible and giving the city’s air a hazy, unclear appearance.

items.stem: Which of the following mixtures are correctly classified as homogeneous (Hm) and heterogeneous (Ht)? Choose the correct option. (i) Air — Hm, Milk — Ht, Sugar solution — Hm, Smoke — Hm (ii) Brass — Ht, Fog — Ht, Vinegar — Ht, Muddy water — Hm (iii) Copper sulfate solution — Hm, Salt solution — Hm, Milk — Hm, Bronze — Hm (iv) Muddy water — Ht, Milk — Ht, Blood — Ht, Brass — Hm
items.answer: Option (iv) is the correct choice. Muddy water, milk, and blood are all heterogeneous mixtures (specifically suspensions or colloids) because their compositions are not uniform throughout, whereas brass is an alloy, which is considered a homogeneous mixture of metals.

items.stem: Choose the correct options, and explain the reason for the correct and incorrect options. Which among the following mixtures show the Tyndall Effect? A mixture of: (a) air and dust particles (b) copper sulfate and water (c) starch and water (d) acetone and water (i) a and b (ii) b and d (iii) a and c (iv) c and d
items.answer: Option (iii) a and c is correct. The Tyndall effect is the scattering of a beam of light by particles in a colloid or fine suspension. A mixture of air and dust particles (an aerosol) and a mixture of starch and water are both colloids, possessing particles large enough to scatter light, making them correct options. On the other hand, copper sulfate in water and acetone in water form true solutions; their solute particles are too small (less than 1 nm in diameter) to scatter light, making them incorrect options.

items.stem: A mixture can be categorised as a solution, a suspension, or a colloid, each possessing distinct properties. Utilise the words or phrases provided in the box to fill in the Table. Words and phrases may be used more than once. Words and Phrases: Large-sized particles; Particles remain evenly distributed; Small-sized particles (less than 1 nm diameter); Moderate-sized particles (1–1000 nm); Settles down when left undisturbed (more than 1000 nm in diameter); Does not settle down; Scatters light; Separates by filtration; Transparent; Salt solution; Milk; Sand in water; Smoke; Heterogeneous mixture; Cannot be separated by filtration; Mud; Butter; Brass. Complete the Table by giving the Properties and the Examples for each of Solution, Suspension and Colloid.
items.answer: Solution — Properties: homogeneous mixture; particle size less than 1 nm (small particles); transparent; particles do not scatter light; stable, particles do not settle down; cannot be separated by filtration. Examples: salt solution, sugar solution. Suspension — Properties: heterogeneous mixture; particle size more than 1000 nm (large particles); opaque; particles scatter light strongly; unstable, particles settle down on standing; can be separated by filtration. Examples: muddy water, sand in water. Colloid — Properties: heterogeneous (appears homogeneous); particle size between 1 nm and 1000 nm; translucent; particles scatter light (Tyndall effect); quite stable, particles do not settle down; cannot be separated by ordinary filtration. Examples: milk, butter, smoke.

items.stem: Solve the following problems: (i) A cake recipe uses dry ingredients, namely 75 g of sugar for 420 g of all-purpose flour and 5 g of sodium hydrogencarbonate. Express the concentration of each component in the mixture using an appropriate method. (ii) A brass alloy contains 70% copper by mass. Calculate the quantities of copper and zinc present in 120 g of brass.
items.answer: (i) We can use the mass by mass percentage (% m/m) method. First, calculate the total mass of the mixture: 75 g (sugar) + 420 g (flour) + 5 g (sodium hydrogencarbonate) = 500 g. Concentration of sugar = (Mass of sugar / Total mass) × 100 = (75 / 500) × 100 = 15% m/m. Concentration of all-purpose flour = (Mass of flour / Total mass) × 100 = (420 / 500) × 100 = 84% m/m. Concentration of sodium hydrogencarbonate = (Mass of sodium hydrogencarbonate / Total mass) × 100 = (5 / 500) × 100 = 1% m/m. (ii) Mass of the brass alloy is 120 g. Quantity of copper = 70% of total mass = (70 / 100) × 120 g = 84 g. Assuming the rest of the alloy is zinc, the percentage of zinc is 100% - 70% = 30%. Quantity of zinc = 30% of total mass = (30 / 100) × 120 g = 36 g (alternatively, 120 g total - 84 g copper = 36 g zinc).

items.stem: The label on a cooking oil pack says one litre (910 g). If this oil is mixed with water, will it form a separate layer? If so, which substance will be on top? How will you separate the two layers? Also, draw the diagram of the apparatus used.
items.answer: Yes, the oil and water will form separate layers because they are immiscible liquids. Based on the label, the density of the oil is 910 g per 1000 mL (0.91 g/mL), which is less than the density of water (approximately 1 g/mL). Because it is lighter, the cooking oil will float and form the top layer. The two layers can be separated using a separating funnel.

items.stem: Assertion (A): Solutions do not exhibit the Tyndall effect. Reason (R): The particles in solutions are larger than 100 nm, so they cannot scatter light. Choose the correct option: (i) Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A. (ii) Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A. (iii) A is true, but R is false. (iv) A is false, but R is true.
items.answer: Option (iii) is the correct choice. The assertion is true because true solutions are homogeneous mixtures that do not scatter light. However, the reason is false because the solute particles in a solution are extremely small (less than 1 nm in diameter), not larger than 100 nm; it is precisely their small size that prevents them from scattering a light beam.

items.stem: How would you separate the mixtures given in Table? Mention the reason for choosing your method. If a mixture cannot be separated, explain why. The table lists, against the columns Mixture, Method of separation and Reason for selection: mud from muddy water; plasma from other components in the blood sample; naphthalene and sand; chalk powder and common salt; common salt and water; oil from water; pigments of the flower.
items.answer:
Mud from muddy water — Filtration. Mud particles are insoluble solids suspended in the water and are large enough to be retained by a filter paper.
Plasma from other components in the blood sample — Centrifugation. Spinning the blood at high speeds applies centrifugal force, causing the heavier blood cells to settle at the bottom while the lighter liquid plasma remains at the top due to density differences.
Naphthalene and sand — Sublimation. Naphthalene is a sublimable substance that transitions directly from a solid to a vapour on heating, leaving the non-sublimable sand behind.
Chalk powder and common salt — Dissolution in water followed by filtration. Common salt is soluble in water while chalk powder is insoluble. After dissolving the salt, filtration separates the solid chalk, and the pure salt can be recovered later by evaporating the filtrate.
Common salt and water — Evaporation. Heating the solution causes the volatile solvent (water) to vaporize, leaving behind the non-volatile solid solute (common salt).
Oil from water — Separating funnel. Oil and water are immiscible liquids with different densities, meaning they do not mix and naturally separate into distinct layers that can be drained off one by one.
Pigments of the flower — Paper chromatography. The different coloured pigments have varying degrees of solubility in the solvent; as the solvent travels up the chromatography paper, the more soluble pigments move faster and separate from the others.

items.answer: Since A and B are miscible liquids with a boiling point difference of 30 °C (which is greater than the required 25 °C minimum difference), they can be successfully separated using the process of simple distillation.

items.stem: Compare evaporation, crystallization and distillation. In which situation, would you prefer each of these over the others?
items.answer: Comparison: 1. Evaporation involves heating a solution to vaporize the volatile solvent, leaving behind a non-volatile solid residue. 2. Crystallization involves slowly cooling a hot, saturated solution so that the solid solute separates out as pure, regular geometric crystals. 3. Distillation involves heating a liquid mixture until the component with the lower boiling point vaporizes, then routing that vapour through a condenser to cool it back into a liquid state for collection. Situations for preference: 1. Evaporation is preferred when you only need to recover a simple, heat-stable solid solute from a solution and do not care about capturing the solvent that evaporates away. 2. Crystallization is preferred over evaporation when obtaining a highly pure solid is necessary, especially if the solid might decompose upon dry heating (like sugar) or if soluble impurities need to be left behind in the remaining liquid. 3. Distillation is preferred when you need to separate and recover both the liquid solvent and the solid solute, or when you need to separate two miscible liquids that have a sufficient difference in their boiling points (at least 25 °C).

items.stem: Blood is an example of a colloidal mixture. (i) What would happen if blood behaved like a true suspension inside the body? (ii) In a blood sample, identify the dispersed phase and the dispersion medium.
items.answer: (i) If blood were a true suspension, the heavier blood cells would settle out of the liquid due to gravity whenever blood flow slowed or stopped. This would lead to blockages in blood vessels, prevent oxygen and nutrients from reaching tissues, and ultimately cause the circulatory system to fail. (ii) In a blood sample, the dispersed phase consists of the blood cells (such as red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets), and the dispersion medium is the liquid plasma in which they are suspended.

items.stem: You are given a mixture of sand, common salt and naphthalene. The figure depicts various steps used to separate the components of this mixture. Identify and write down the correct sequence of separation techniques.
items.answer: Based on the visual cues in the figure the correct sequence of separation techniques is: 1. Sublimation (heating the mixture with an inverted funnel to separate the sublimable naphthalene). 2. Filtration (pouring the remaining mixture, after adding water to dissolve the salt, through filter paper to remove the insoluble sand). 3. Evaporation (heating the collected filtrate in a dish to boil off the water and leave behind the common salt).

items.stem: Why is distillation an effective method for separating a mixture of water and acetone?
items.answer: Distillation is effective because water and acetone are miscible liquids with a large difference in their boiling points. Acetone boils at approximately 56 °C, while water boils at 100 °C. Because this difference (44 °C) is greater than 25 °C, the acetone readily vaporizes first upon heating and can be condensed and collected as a pure liquid well before the water begins to vaporize significantly.

items.stem: Answer the following questions with the help of the data given in the Table. Table: solubility of various salts, in g per 100 g of water, at 10 °C, 20 °C, 30 °C, 40 °C, 60 °C and 80 °C respectively — Potassium nitrate: 21, 32, 45, 62, 106, 167; Sodium chloride: 36, 36, 36.3, 36.5, 37, 37; Potassium chloride: 35, 35, 37.4, 40, 46, 54; Ammonium chloride: 24, 37, 41, 41, 55, 66. (i) What mass of potassium nitrate would be needed to prepare its saturated solution in 50 g of water at 40 °C? (ii) A student makes a saturated solution of potassium chloride in water at 80 °C and leaves the solution to cool at room temperature (25 °C). What would she observe as the solution cools? Explain. (iii) What is the effect of a change in temperature on the solubility of salts? Also, compare the changes in the solubility of the four given salts with increasing temperature from 10 °C to 80 °C.
items.answer:
(i) According to the table, the solubility of potassium nitrate at 40 °C is 62 g per 100 g of water. To prepare a saturated solution in half that amount of water (50 g), you would need half the mass of the salt, which is 31 g of potassium nitrate.
(ii) She would observe solid crystals forming in the solution. This happens because the solubility of solid salts generally decreases as temperature drops. The water can hold 54 g of potassium chloride at 80 °C but only around 36 g at 25 °C, forcing the excess dissolved salt to separate out of the solution in crystalline form.
(iii) Generally, an increase in temperature increases the solubility of solid salts in water. Comparing the given salts from 10 °C to 80 °C: Potassium nitrate shows a massive increase in solubility (from 21 g to 167 g). Ammonium chloride and Potassium chloride show steady, moderate increases in solubility. Sodium chloride is unique among the four, as its solubility shows almost no change, remaining relatively constant (increasing slightly from 36 g to 37 g).

items.stem: Three students, A, B and C, are preparing sugar solutions for an experiment. Student A dissolves 20 g of sugar in 80 g of water. Student B dissolves 20 g of sugar in 100 g of water. Student C dissolves 30 g of sugar in 80 g of water. (i) Calculate the mass percentage (% m/m) concentration of sugar in each student’s solution. (ii) Whose solution is the most concentrated? Explain why.
items.answer:
(i) The mass percentage is the mass of the solute divided by the total mass of the solution, multiplied by one hundred. Student A dissolved 20 g of sugar in 80 g of water, so that solution has a total mass of one hundred grams and its concentration is 20 per cent m/m. Student B dissolved 20 g of sugar in 100 g of water, so that solution has a total mass of one hundred and twenty grams and its concentration is 16.67 per cent m/m. Student C dissolved 30 g of sugar in 80 g of water, so that solution has a total mass of one hundred and ten grams and its concentration is 27.27 per cent m/m.
(ii) Student C’s solution is the most concentrated. This is because it has the highest mass percentage (27.27 per cent), meaning it contains the highest proportion of solute relative to the total mass of the solution compared to the mixtures prepared by students A and B.

items.answer: A homogeneous mixture is defined by its uniform composition throughout its entire volume. In these types of mixtures, individual components completely mix and are never visibly distinct from one another. A classic everyday example is common salt dissolved in water. This solution remains homogeneous, and the solute never settles down when left completely undisturbed.

items.stem: Which of the following statements correctly describes a saturated solution?
items.answer: A saturated solution is strictly defined as a solution that cannot dissolve any additional amount of solute at a specific given temperature. Once this maximum capacity is reached, any extra solid solute added will simply remain undissolved and settle at the bottom of the container, maintaining the equilibrium of the chemical mixture.

items.answer: If the thoroughly confused student foolishly attempted to desperately use a standard glass separating funnel to perfectly separate a prepared mixture of pure acetone and liquid alcohol, the flawed method would absolutely fail instantly, granting zero physical separation. A standard separating funnel intrinsically relies entirely strictly upon the basic fundamental physical principle of massively distinct liquid density differences existing strictly between two purely immiscible liquids that completely refuse to organically mix. However, both liquid acetone and liquid alcohol are extremely highly miscible, freely dissolving permanently into a totally inseparable single phase.

items.stem: Explain clearly how the extremely important fundamental physical principle of biological mixture separation is naturally utilized continuously by the internal human body and heavily by large scale modern municipal wastewater sewage treatment plants.
items.answer: The highly essential physical principle of complex mixture separation is absolutely vital for continuously sustaining healthy internal organic life and heavily maintaining our external environment. Deep inside the internal human body, truly vital organic organs exactly like our twin kidneys continuously act essentially as highly complex microscopic biological filters, incredibly efficiently and safely separating toxic chemical waste products entirely from our rapidly circulating blood. Similarly, massively large scale modern municipal wastewater sewage treatment plants heavily rely absolutely upon extremely massive separation techniques including thick sedimentation, intense coagulation, and rapid physical filtration completely.

items.stem: Draw a simple laboratory setup perfectly showing the absolute endpoint of a successful paper chromatography experiment specifically for testing a green plant leaf extract. Why exactly is plain water or alcohol fundamentally able to carry pigments upwards?
items.answer: The selected liquid chemical solvent, whether simple plain liquid water or a harsh chemical alcohol, is completely miraculously successfully able to easily physically carry the various incredibly diverse dissolved coloured organic pigments heavily upward completely defying gravity entirely due to an extremely incredibly important natural physical phenomenon scientifically known strictly as capillary action. As the incredibly dense liquid slowly seamlessly soaks deeply and heavily rises actively through the completely microscopic internal porous fibres of the paper, it continuously vigorously drags the lighter dissolved dye molecules vertically upward entirely at totally varying different speeds.

items.stem: (a) Explain the entire process of obtaining pure copper sulfate crystals from an impure laboratory sample, accompanied by a diagram showing the cooling phase of the hot saturated solution? (b) Why is crystallization considered a significantly better technique than simple evaporation to dryness for purifying such solid mixtures?
items.answer: (a) To obtain pure copper sulfate, dissolve the impure sample in a minimum amount of water with a drop of dilute sulfuric acid. Heat the mixture gently to prepare a saturated solution. Filter this hot liquid to remove insoluble impurities. Finally, allow the clear filtrate to cool slowly without disturbance. As the temperature drops, solubility decreases, and pure copper sulfate particles arrange into geometric solid crystals, leaving soluble impurities behind in the remaining liquid. (b) Crystallization is vastly superior to simple evaporation to dryness for two main reasons. Firstly, direct heating during evaporation can cause certain sensitive solids to decompose or char completely. Secondly, evaporation leaves all soluble impurities mixed directly with the newly dried solid. Crystallization successfully isolates the pure compound because the soluble impurities remain fully dissolved within the leftover solvent instead of incorporating into the newly formed solid crystal lattice.

items.stem: (a) Describe a detailed activity using paper chromatography to definitively show that black sketch pen ink is not a single individual colour? (b) State the fundamental basic principle of separation utilised in this specific technique? (c) Will the separation pattern remain exactly the same if liquid alcohol is used as a solvent instead of water?
items.answer: (a) To prove black ink is a mixture, draw a horizontal pencil line near the bottom of a filter paper strip and place a small spot of black ink precisely on its centre. Suspend this paper strip vertically inside a glass jar containing a small amount of water, ensuring the water level remains just below the ink spot. As the water slowly rises up the paper via capillary action, it carries the ink dyes along with it, separating into multiple distinct coloured bands. (b) This technique relies on the principle that different components of a mixture possess different solubilities in a given solvent and interact differently with the stationary paper. Consequently, they travel upward at varying speeds. (c) If alcohol is substituted for water, the separation pattern will change significantly because dye solubilities will differ entirely in the new solvent.

items.stem: (a) Define the specific terms sublimation and deposition as they relate to changes in states of matter? (b) You are given a complex mixture of camphor, sand, and common salt. Propose a logical, sequential methodology to separate these three distinct components completely from one another?
items.answer: (a) Sublimation is the unique physical process where a solid changes directly into a vapour upon heating, completely bypassing the liquid state. Deposition is the exact reverse process, where a vapour cools and transforms directly back into a solid without becoming a liquid. (b) To separate the given mixture, follow a sequential physical methodology. First, gently heat the entire mixture in a china dish covered with an inverted funnel. The camphor will undergo sublimation and deposit onto the cool inner walls of the funnel, separating it entirely. Second, add water to the remaining sand and salt mixture and stir thoroughly. The common salt will dissolve completely, while the sand remains insoluble. Filter the mixture to collect the sand as the solid residue. Finally, gently evaporate the clear filtrate to remove the water, leaving pure solid common salt behind.

items.stem: (a) Define a saturated solution? (b) Why is temperature strictly specified when defining the solubility of a substance? (c) A student dissolves 15 g of common salt in 85 g of water. Calculate the mass by mass percentage of the solution? (d) What happens if a saturated solution of a solid in liquid is heated?
items.answer:
(a) A saturated solution is a solution in which no more solute can be dissolved in the solvent at a specific given temperature.
(b) Temperature is strictly specified because the solubility of a solid solute in a liquid solvent generally increases as the temperature rises. Thus, a solution saturated at one temperature may become unsaturated when heated.
(c) For the mathematical calculation:
Mass of the solute (common salt) = 15 g
Mass of the solvent (water) = 85 g
Total mass of the solution = Mass of solute + Mass of solvent = 15 g + 85 g = 100 g
Mass by mass percentage = (Mass of solute / Mass of solution) × 100 = (15/100) × 100 = 15%
(d) Heating a saturated solution increases its kinetic energy, allowing it to dissolve even more solute.

items.stem: (a) How would you separate a mixture of mustard oil and water? (b) Explain the foundational principle behind the specific technique used? (c) If two completely immiscible liquids having the exact same density are mixed together, can they be separated using this standard apparatus? Justify your reasoning?
items.answer:
(a) To separate a mixture of mustard oil and water, one must use a separating funnel apparatus.
(b) The fundamental principle behind this technique is that immiscible liquids do not mix and will naturally separate into distinct layers depending upon their respective densities. Because water is denser than mustard oil, water settles at the bottom of the funnel, while the lighter mustard oil forms the upper layer. You carefully open the stopcock to collect the water layer first, closing it just before the oil reaches the bottom.
(c) If two immiscible liquids possess the exact same density, they cannot be successfully separated using a basic separating funnel. Since gravity pulls equally on both liquids relative to their volume, neither liquid will inherently sink or float. Without a density difference, clear top and bottom layers will never form, rendering this gravitational separation useless.

items.stem: (a) Draw a labelled diagram of the apparatus used to separate a mixture of acetone and water? (b) Explain the scientific principle behind this separation technique? (c) Why is this method highly suitable for separating acetone and water but not for separating crude petroleum components?
items.answer:
(a) [Labelled diagram of the simple distillation apparatus.]
(b) The basic principle of simple distillation relies on a significant difference in the boiling points of two miscible liquids. The mixture is heated until the liquid with the lower boiling point vaporizes. These vapours travel into a condenser where they are cooled back into a liquid state and collected separately, leaving the higher boiling point liquid behind in the distillation flask.
(c) This specific separation method is highly suitable for an acetone and water mixture because their boiling points differ by more than twenty-five degrees Celsius. Acetone boils at fifty-six degrees Celsius, while water boils at one hundred degrees Celsius. However, petroleum components have very closely spaced boiling points, usually differing by less than twenty-five degrees Celsius. Therefore, simple distillation fails to separate them purely, and complex fractional distillation must be used instead to isolate the petroleum fractions.

items.stem: (a) What is the Tyndall effect? (b) Why does a true homogeneous solution absolutely fail to show this visual effect? (c) Differentiate between a colloid and a suspension specifically based on particle size and settling behaviour? (d) Finally, identify the dispersed phase and dispersion medium in atmospheric clouds?
items.answer:
(a) The Tyndall effect is the phenomenon where a beam of light becomes visible as it passes through a medium because the particles in that medium scatter the light.
(b) A true solution does not exhibit this effect because its dissolved solute particles are incredibly small, measuring less than one nanometre in diameter, which is insufficient to scatter visible light waves.
(c) A colloid differs from a suspension primarily in particle size and stability. Colloidal particles range between one and one thousand nanometres and remain uniformly distributed without settling down over time. In contrast, suspension particles are larger than one thousand nanometres and are unstable, settling down at the bottom due to gravity when left undisturbed.
(d) In the specific case of clouds, the dispersed phase consists of liquid water droplets or solid ice crystals, while the dispersion medium is the surrounding gaseous air.

items.stem: (a) How exactly does the process of centrifugation help in separating microscopic particles from a liquid mixture? (b) Mention one critical application of this technique in the modern medical field? (c) If a sample of muddy water remains distinctly cloudy even after standard filtration, how can you rapidly clear it using coagulation?
items.answer:
(a) Centrifugation separates complex mixtures by spinning them rapidly inside an electric machine. This rapid rotation generates a strong outward centrifugal force. The heavier, denser solid particles are forced forcefully outward and settle rapidly at the bottom of the test tube, while the much lighter liquid components remain suspended at the top.
(b) A primary application in the medical field is separating whole blood into distinct layers of red blood cells, platelets, and clear plasma for diagnostic testing.
(c) When muddy water remains cloudy despite traditional filtration, the tiny suspended particles can be separated utilising chemical coagulation. By adding powdered alum to the cloudy liquid, the alum acts directly as a coagulant. It causes the microscopic, suspended clay particles to clump together into significantly larger, heavier masses. These heavy clumps then settle downward efficiently by gravity, allowing clear water decantation.

items.stem: (a) Draw a labelled flowchart or schematic diagram illustrating the primary products obtained from the fractional distillation of crude oil? (b) How does fractional distillation fundamentally differ from simple distillation in terms of its application parameters? (c) Why must raw crude petroleum be separated using this specific, complex technique?
items.answer:
(a) [Labelled flowchart of the fractions obtained from the fractional distillation of crude oil.]
(b) Fractional distillation is specifically utilised to separate liquid mixtures where the boiling points of the miscible components differ by a very narrow margin, specifically less than twenty-five degrees Celsius. Simple distillation is entirely ineffective here and is only used when the boiling point difference is substantial.
(c) Crude petroleum is an incredibly complex mixture of numerous valuable hydrocarbon liquids. Because these various components, such as petrol, diesel, and kerosene, have densely packed boiling points, simple evaporation and condensation would produce heavily mixed, impure liquids. To resolve this, crude oil is processed in a massive fractional distillation column. The oil is vaporized entirely, and as the vapours rise up the tall column, it slowly cools. Different fractions condense at highly specific height zones based directly on their unique boiling points, allowing the simultaneous collection of multiple pure industrial fuels.

items.stem: (a) A concentrated liquid pesticide spray is heavily diluted by mixing 25 mL of the active pesticide with pure water to make a total volume of 500 mL. Calculate its final volume by volume percentage? (b) Explain exactly what an emulsion is, providing an everyday example, and explain how emulsifying agents function?
items.answer:
(a) To calculate the concentration properly, use the standard volume by volume percentage formula. The volume of the solute, which is the concentrated pesticide, equals twenty-five millilitres. The total combined volume of the final aqueous solution is given as five hundred millilitres. The mass by volume percentage equals the solute volume divided by the total solution volume, multiplied by one hundred. Therefore, dividing twenty-five by five hundred yields zero point zero five. Multiplying this by one hundred results in a final concentration of exactly five percent.
(b) An emulsion is a distinct category of colloidal mixture where both the dispersed phase and the surrounding dispersion medium are mutually immiscible liquids. Everyday milk is a perfect example. Emulsifying agents, such as natural milk proteins, effectively stabilize these mixtures by preventing the suspended liquid droplets from aggressively coalescing and separating into distinct layers.

During a school play, the drama club used a smoke machine to create a thick, mysterious fog on stage. As the stage lights turned on, the audience could clearly see the bright, solid-looking beams of light piercing through the fog. Meanwhile, one of the actors was holding a glass of a clear, purple-coloured sports drink as a prop. When a stray spotlight hit the glass, the light passed straight through it, but no beam was visible inside the purple liquid itself.
QUESTIONS:
(a) Classify the fog on the stage and the sports drink in the glass as homogeneous or heterogeneous mixtures.
(b) What is the scientific name for the phenomenon that makes the light beams visible in the stage fog?
(c) Why was the path of the light beam visible in the fog but not in the clear sports drink?
(d) Based on particle size, what specific type of mixture is the fog likely to be?
items.answer:
(a) The fog is a heterogeneous mixture, while the clear sports drink is a homogeneous mixture (a solution).
(b) The phenomenon is known as the Tyndall effect, which is the scattering of light by particles.
(c) The particles in the fog are large enough to scatter the light, making the beam’s path visible. The sports drink is a true solution with particles less than 1 nm in diameter, which are too small to scatter light.
(d) The fog is a colloid (or an aerosol, which is a specific type of colloid with a gas as the dispersion medium).

items.stem:
During a local marathon in the summer, a medical volunteer named Priya is tasked with preparing rehydration fluids for the runners. She needs to prepare a specific glucose drip for a runner who has collapsed from exhaustion. The doctor instructs her to quickly prepare 300 mL of a 5% m/v (mass by volume percentage) glucose solution. Priya has a large container of pure glucose powder and several bottles of sterile distilled water at her medical station.
QUESTIONS:
(a) Identify the solute and the solvent in the mixture Priya is preparing.
(b) Calculate the exact mass of glucose powder Priya needs to measure out to prepare 300 mL of the required 5% m/v solution.
(c) Why is it important for Priya to mix the exact right proportion of glucose and water, rather than just guessing the amounts?
items.answer:
(a) The solute is the glucose powder, and the solvent is the sterile distilled water.
(b) Mass by volume percentage is the mass of the solute divided by the volume of the solution, multiplied by one hundred. Putting five per cent for the concentration and 300 mL for the volume of the solution, the mass of glucose needed is five multiplied by three hundred and then divided by one hundred, which is 15 grams. Priya needs 15 grams of glucose.
(c) The proportion has to be exact because the concentration is what makes the drip work safely. Too little glucose would not replace the energy and the fluid the collapsed runner has lost, while too much would make the solution more concentrated than the body’s own fluids and would draw water out of the cells instead of rehydrating them. A stated concentration such as 5% m/v is a fixed recipe, so guessing the amounts would give a different solution every time.

A local sweet-shop owner (halwai) is preparing thick sugar syrup, locally known as chashni, for making traditional sweets. He pours a massive amount of sugar into a vat of water and begins to heat it over a stove. Even though the water initially couldn’t dissolve all the sugar, as the temperature rises, the sugar disappears completely into the liquid. After dipping the sweets, he turns off the stove and lets the leftover syrup sit overnight. By the next morning, he notices that solid sugar crystals have formed on the bottom and sides of the vat.
QUESTIONS:
(a) What term describes the hot sugar syrup when it cannot dissolve any more sugar at that specific high temperature?
(b) Why was the halwai able to dissolve extra sugar in the water by heating it?
(c) Explain why the solid sugar crystals reappeared in the vat the next morning.
items.answer:
(a) The syrup is called a saturated solution at that specific temperature.
(b) He was able to dissolve more sugar because the solubility of a solid solute in a liquid solvent generally increases with an increase in temperature.
(c) As the syrup cooled overnight, the temperature dropped, causing the solubility of the sugar to decrease. The extra sugar that could no longer stay dissolved separated out from the solution as solid crystals.

items.stem:
While working in his garage, a mechanic accidentally knocks a small bottle of yellow engine oil into a bucket of water. Knowing that engine oil is expensive, he wants to recover as much of the pure oil as possible. He notices that the oil and water do not mix, and after a few minutes of standing undisturbed, a distinct yellow layer forms on top of the clear water. He remembers a lesson from his school days about a specific piece of laboratory glass equipment that operates on this exact principle.
QUESTIONS:
(a) What type of mixture is formed when the engine oil spills into the water?
(b) Name the laboratory apparatus that the mechanic could use to efficiently separate these two liquids if he were in a science lab.
(c) Why does the engine oil form the upper layer while the water forms the lower layer?
(d) Briefly describe the steps he would take using the laboratory apparatus to collect the water and oil separately.
items.answer:
(a) It is a heterogeneous mixture of two immiscible liquids.
(b) A separating funnel can be used to separate them.
(c) Oil forms the upper layer because it has a lower density than water, causing it to float on top.
(d) He would pour the mixture into the separating funnel and let it stand so the layers separate. Then, he would open the stopcock to drain the lower water layer into a flask, close it when the water is drained, and then collect the remaining oil in a separate container.

items.stem:
Before the onset of winter, Rohan’s grandmother brings out heavy woolen blankets from an old wooden trunk. Rohan notices a strong smell and sees that his grandmother is placing small, white naphthalene balls between the folds of the blankets before putting them away again in the spring. Six months later, when the blankets are unpacked again, Rohan looks for the white balls to throw them away, but he cannot find them. There are no liquid stains on the blankets either. The balls seem to have vanished entirely.
QUESTIONS:
(a) What specific physical change caused the naphthalene balls to vanish without leaving wet stains?
(b) Define the process identified in CBQ1.
(c) If Rohan mixed crushed naphthalene with normal sand by mistake, how could he separate the sand from the naphthalene?
(d) Name one other common substance, often used in ice cream storage, that undergoes this same process.
(e) Is the melting of an ice cube the same type of physical change as the vanishing of the naphthalene balls? Justify your answer.
items.answer:
(a) The naphthalene balls underwent sublimation. The solid changed directly into vapour and escaped into the air, so no liquid was ever formed and no wet stains were left behind.
(b) Sublimation is the physical process in which a solid changes directly into a vapour on heating, completely bypassing the intermediate liquid state.
(c) He could heat the mixture gently in a china dish covered with an inverted funnel. The naphthalene would sublime and then deposit as solid crystals on the cool inner walls of the funnel, leaving the sand behind in the dish.
(d) Dry ice, which is solid carbon dioxide, also sublimes and is commonly used in ice cream storage.
(e) No. Melting is a change from the solid state to the liquid state, whereas the naphthalene balls sublimed, changing directly from the solid state to the vapour state without ever becoming a liquid. Both are physical changes, but they are not the same type of change of state.

items.stem:
A forensics student is investigating a case of a forged signature on a cheque. The suspect claims the signature was written using a standard black sketch pen found in the office. The student decides to test the ink. She places a tiny spot of ink from the cheque onto a thin strip of specialized filter paper. She carefully suspends the paper in a beaker containing a small amount of water, ensuring the ink spot sits just above the water level. After twenty minutes, she observes a beautiful band of blue, yellow, and red streaks climbing up the paper.
QUESTIONS:
(a) Identify the scientific technique being used by the forensics student to analyze the ink.
(b) What can the student infer about the black ink based on the coloured streaks on the paper?
(c) Explain the basic principle that allows the different colours to separate on the paper.
(d) Why was it crucial for the student to keep the ink spot slightly above the water level at the beginning of the experiment?
items.answer:
(a) The technique is paper chromatography.
(b) The student can infer that the black ink is not a single pure substance, but a homogeneous mixture of multiple coloured components (dyes).
(c) The separation is based on differences in the interactions of the components with the solvent and the paper. As the solvent (water) rises, it carries the dyes with it at different speeds, separating them.
(d) If the ink spot was submerged in the water, the ink would simply dissolve into the bulk of the water at the bottom of the beaker instead of travelling up the paper strip.

During a practical exam, a student accidentally pours acetone into a flask that contains pure distilled water. Acetone is highly miscible in water, resulting in a perfectly clear mixture. The teacher informs the student that the boiling point of water is 100 °C, while the boiling point of acetone is much lower, at 56 °C. She challenges the student to set up an apparatus to recover both liquids in their pure forms without losing either to the atmosphere.
QUESTIONS:
(a) Name the process the student should use to separate this mixture of miscible liquids.
(b) Why is this specific separation process effective for the acetone and water mixture?
(c) As the mixture is heated, which liquid will turn into vapour first, and why?
(d) What is the role of the water condenser in this apparatus?
(e) If the student had mixed two liquids with boiling points of 75 °C and 78 °C, could this exact same simple setup be used effectively? Explain.
items.answer:
(a) The student should use the distillation process.
(b) Distillation is effective because acetone and water are miscible liquids that boil without decomposition and have a sufficient difference in their boiling points (greater than 25 °C).
(c) Acetone will vaporize first because it has a lower boiling point (56 °C) compared to water (100 °C).
(d) The condenser cools the hot vapours of the vaporized liquid (acetone) by circulating cold water around it, turning the vapour back into a liquid so it can be collected in a separate flask.
(e) No, simple distillation would not be effective because the difference in boiling points is less than 25 °C. For such closely boiling liquids, a fractional distillation setup would be required.

Dr. Ahmed runs a mobile clinic in a remote village with frequent power cuts. He needs to test blood samples for anemia by separating the heavier red blood cells from the lighter plasma. Since he cannot use an electric machine, he uses a ‘paperfuge’—a simple disk made of cardboard and string that he spins rapidly by pulling the strings. In another part of the village, a farmer is using a piece of alum (fitkari) to clean buckets of highly muddy river water, waiting for the fine dirt to clump and settle.
QUESTIONS:
(a) What is the separation technique Dr. Ahmed is imitating with his hand-powered paperfuge?
(b) State the fundamental principle behind Dr. Ahmed’s separation technique.
(c) According to the textbook, how is a blood mixture classified?
(d) What is the scientific term for the process the farmer is using to clear the muddy water?
(e) How exactly does the alum (fitkari) help in cleaning the farmer’s muddy water?
items.answer:
(a) Dr. Ahmed is using centrifugation.
(b) The principle is that when a mixture is spun rapidly, centrifugal force pushes the heavier particles to the bottom (or outward), while the lighter components remain at the top (or center).
(c) Blood is classified as a colloid.
(d) The process is called coagulation.
(e) Alum acts as a coagulant. It causes the fine suspended mud particles, which would otherwise take a long time to settle, to clump together into larger, heavier masses that easily settle down at the bottom by gravity.

items.stem:
A local dairy cooperative produces fresh paneer (cottage cheese) every morning. To make the paneer, workers heat large vats of fresh milk and add natural lemon juice. Almost immediately, the uniform liquid begins to separate into solid white curds and a watery, greenish-yellow liquid called whey. The heavy curds are then strained through a clean muslin cloth, pressed to remove excess water, and sold in blocks.
QUESTIONS:
(a) What scientific process occurs when lemon juice is added to the milk to form the curds?
(b) What role does the lemon juice play in this process?
(c) What separation technique is used when the workers pass the curd and whey mixture through the muslin cloth?
items.answer:
(a) The process is called coagulation (specifically, the coagulation of milk proteins).
(b) The lemon juice (which contains acid) acts as a coagulant, causing the proteins in the milk to clump together into larger solid masses (curds).
(c) The separation technique used with the muslin cloth is filtration.

items.stem:
A class of Grade 9 students visits a factory that processes salt harvested from the sea. The guide explains that the initial salt obtained by evaporating seawater in open pans contains a lot of unwanted dirt, grit, and other chemical impurities. To purify it, the factory dissolves this impure salt in hot water to make a highly concentrated solution, filters it, and then allows the hot solution to cool slowly in large stainless-steel tanks. Eventually, brilliant, pure white geometric shapes of salt begin to form at the bottom of the tanks.
QUESTIONS:
(a) What is the scientific name for the pure, geometric shapes of solid salt forming at the bottom of the tanks?
(b) Identify the technique used by the factory to obtain the pure solid salt from the hot, concentrated solution.
(c) Why is it necessary to filter the hot solution before allowing it to cool?
(d) Why is the factory’s cooling technique considered a better purification method than simply boiling the saltwater mixture until all the water evaporates (dryness)?
items.answer:
(a) They are called crystals.
(b) The technique is crystallization.
(c) Filtration of the hot solution is necessary to remove the insoluble impurities (like dirt and grit) before the pure crystals start to form.
(d) Crystallization is better than simple evaporation to dryness because evaporation might leave soluble impurities mixed with the solid, whereas crystallization specifically separates the pure substance as crystals, leaving the soluble impurities behind in the remaining liquid.
